title: 11. Projects: Day 16 — Human-in-the-Loop
summary: A drafter agent writes an email from a request. The graph then pauses at a human_review node using interrupt() from langgraph.types.
objectives: Build the Day 16 — Human-in-the-Loop projects end to end
Keep a short README with assumptions and tradeoffs

sections.title: Project 1 — Approval-Required Email Sender (LangGraph)
sections.body:
### Overview

A drafter agent writes an email from a request. The graph then **pauses** at a `human_review` node using `interrupt()` from `langgraph.types`. The human sees the draft in the terminal and types one of `approve`, `revise <feedback>`, or `abort`. The graph is resumed with `Command(resume=...)`, which delivers the human's decision back into the node where `interrupt()` was called. A `MemorySaver` checkpointer persists state across the pause so the graph can be resumed in a later process if you want.

### Full Code

```python
"""
Approval-Required Email Sender — LangGraph HITL using interrupt().
Run:  python day16_email_approval.py
"""
from typing import TypedDict, Literal

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, SystemMessage

llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0.4)

# --- State -------------------------------------------------------------

class EmailState(TypedDict):
    request: str          # what the user wants the email to say
    draft: str            # current draft
    feedback: str         # human feedback from review ("" if approved)
    sent: bool
    revision_count: int
    aborted: bool

# --- Nodes -------------------------------------------------------------

def drafter_node(state: EmailState) -> dict:
    """Compose the first draft, or revise based on human feedback."""
    request = state["request"]
    feedback = state.get("feedback", "")
    if feedback:
        prompt = [
            SystemMessage(content=(
                "You revise email drafts based on reviewer feedback. "
                "Keep under 150 words. Return only the revised body."
            )),
            HumanMessage(content=(
                f"Original request: {request}\n\n"
                f"Current draft:\n{state['draft']}\n\n"
                f"Reviewer feedback: {feedback}\n\nRevised email:"
            )),
        ]
    else:
        prompt = [
            SystemMessage(content=(
                "You draft professional emails under 150 words. "
                "Return only the email body (no subject)."
            )),
            HumanMessage(content=f"Request: {request}\n\nDraft:"),
        ]
    draft = llm.invoke(prompt).content
    print(f"\n[drafter] produced draft (rev={state['revision_count']}):\n{draft}\n")
    return {"draft": draft, "feedback": ""}

def human_review_node(state: EmailState) -> dict:
    """Pause execution; the value passed to interrupt() is shown to the human.
    The graph resumes when Command(resume=...) is invoked; the value passed to
    resume becomes the RETURN VALUE of interrupt() here."""
    decision = interrupt({
        "prompt": "Approve this email draft?",
        "draft": state["draft"],
        "revision": state["revision_count"],
    })
    # decision is whatever the caller passed to Command(resume=...)
    action = decision.get("action", "approve")
    print(f"[human] decision: {action}")
    if action == "revise":
        return {
            "feedback": decision.get("feedback", ""),
            "revision_count": state["revision_count"] + 1,
        }
    if action == "abort":
        return {"aborted": True}
    return {}  # approve -> no state change, fall through to sender

def sender_node(state: EmailState) -> dict:
    """Mock sending the approved email."""
    print(f"[sender] sending email:\n{state['draft']}\n")
    # Real life: smtplib.sendmail(...) or third-party API call.
    return {"sent": True}

# --- Routing -----------------------------------------------------------

def route_after_review(state: EmailState) -> Literal["sender", "drafter", "__end__"]:
    if state.get("aborted"):
        return END
    if state.get("feedback"):
        return "drafter"   # revise
    return "sender"        # approved

# --- Graph -------------------------------------------------------------

builder = StateGraph(EmailState)
builder.add_node("drafter", drafter_node)
builder.add_node("human_review", human_review_node)
builder.add_node("sender", sender_node)
builder.add_edge(START, "drafter")
builder.add_edge("drafter", "human_review")
builder.add_conditional_edges("human_review", route_after_review)
builder.add_edge("sender", END)

checkpointer = MemorySaver()
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

# --- Run with a real human in the loop --------------------------------

def run_email_workflow(request: str, thread_id: str = "email-1") -> None:
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}}
    initial = {
        "request": request, "draft": "", "feedback": "",
        "sent": False, "revision_count": 0, "aborted": False,
    }
    # First invoke runs until interrupt() is hit.
    graph.invoke(initial, config=config)

    # Loop: detect interrupt, prompt human, resume, repeat until done.
    while True:
        state = graph.get_state(config)
        if not state.next:
            break  # graph finished

        # Is the next task actually interrupted, or just queued?
        interrupted = any(getattr(t, "interrupts", None) for t in state.tasks)
        if not interrupted:
            graph.invoke(None, config=config)
            continue

        current = state.values
        print("=" * 60)
        print(f"DRAFT (rev #{current['revision_count']}):")
        print(current.get("draft", ""))
        print("=" * 60)
        action = input("Action [approve/revise/abort]: ").strip().lower()
        if action == "revise":
            feedback = input("Feedback: ").strip()
            resume = {"action": "revise", "feedback": feedback}
        elif action == "abort":
            resume = {"action": "abort"}
        else:
            resume = {"action": "approve"}
        graph.invoke(Command(resume=resume), config=config)

    final = graph.get_state(config).values
    print(f"\n[workflow] sent={final.get('sent', False)} "
          f"revisions={final.get('revision_count', 0)} "
          f"aborted={final.get('aborted', False)}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_email_workflow(
        "Tell Alice we'll be 2 weeks late delivering the Q3 report. "
        "Apologize, blame data-quality issues, offer a 5% discount on next invoice."
    )
```

### Walkthrough

**`interrupt()` semantics (lines 53-66).** When `human_review_node` calls `interrupt(payload)`, two things happen: (1) `payload` is captured and exposed to the caller via `graph.get_state(config).tasks[*].interrupts[*].value`, and (2) the graph pauses — control returns to whoever called `graph.invoke()`. The return value of `interrupt()` is *not* `payload`; it is whatever is later passed to `Command(resume=...)`. This is the key abstraction: `interrupt()` is a yield point that blocks until the human answers. Mentally model it as a Python generator's `yield`: the function suspends, returns a value to the caller, and resumes later with a different value sent back in.

**Resuming (lines 96-110).** After the first `invoke`, we enter a loop. `graph.get_state(config).next` lists nodes still queued to run; if empty, the graph is done. `state.tasks[*].interrupts` is non-empty only when the graph is actually paused at an `interrupt()` (as opposed to merely queued). We prompt the human, build a resume payload, and call `graph.invoke(Command(resume=resume), config=config)`. The checkpointer ensures state survives across these multiple invoke calls. A subtlety: the resume payload can be any JSON-serializable value (dict, string, list). We use a dict `{"action": "...", "feedback": "..."}` so a single `interrupt()` call site can carry multiple kinds of human decisions.

**Routing after review (lines 80-84).** Three branches: aborted -> END, has feedback -> back to drafter, approved -> sender. Because we re-enter at `drafter` (which loops through `human_review` again), each revision triggers another approval prompt — exactly what you want. The `aborted` flag is separate from `feedback` because abort is terminal (no more drafting) while feedback means "try again." Conflating them — e.g., using `feedback == "__abort__"` as a sentinel — works but is brittle; explicit flags are easier to grep and reason about.

### Expected Output

```text
[drafter] produced draft (rev=0):
Hi Alice, I'm writing to let you know the Q3 report will be delayed by two weeks...

============================================================
DRAFT (rev #0):
Hi Alice, I'm writing to let you know the Q3 report will be delayed by two weeks...
============================================================
Action [approve/revise/abort]: revise
Feedback: Make it shorter and lead with the apology.

[human] decision: revise
[drafter] produced draft (rev=1):
Hi Alice, Apologies — the Q3 report will be delayed by two weeks due to data-quality issues...

============================================================
DRAFT (rev #1):
Hi Alice, Apologies — the Q3 report will be delayed by two weeks due to data-quality issues...
============================================================
Action [approve/revise/abort]: approve

[human] decision: approve
[sender] sending email:
Hi Alice, Apologies...

[workflow] sent=True revisions=1 aborted=False
```

sections.title: Project 2 — Editable Draft Reviewer (Pydantic AI)
sections.body:
### Overview

Pydantic AI does not have a built-in `interrupt()` primitive like LangGraph; instead you compose HITL in plain Python. The agent uses `agent.iter()` to expose intermediate model requests and tool calls (so you can show progress to the human), and the human turn is a simple `input()`. On "edit", we spawn a refinement agent that takes the prior draft plus the feedback and produces a new draft. The loop continues until the human approves, rejects, or hits a max-revision cap.

### Full Code

```python
"""
Editable Draft Reviewer — Pydantic AI agent + plain-Python HITL loop.
Uses agent.iter() to expose intermediate steps; input() for the human turn.
Run:  python day16_draft_reviewer.py
"""
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator
from pydantic_ai import Agent

# --- Output type ------------------------------------------------------

class Draft(BaseModel):
    title: str
    body: str
    word_count: int = Field(description="Auto-computed: word count of body.")

    @field_validator("word_count")
    @classmethod
    def _check_count(cls, v: int, info) -> int:
        # If body is available, recompute to keep honest.
        body = info.data.get("body", "")
        return len(body.split()) if body else v

class DraftRequest(BaseModel):
    topic: str
    audience: str = "general"
    max_words: int = 200

# --- Agents -----------------------------------------------------------

drafter = Agent(
    "openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    output_type=Draft,
    system_prompt=(
        "You write clean, focused drafts. Match the requested audience and word count. "
        "Set title to a short (3-6 word) header. Recompute word_count from body."
    ),
)

def make_refiner() -> Agent:
    """Build a fresh refiner agent each revision (so its system prompt stays tight)."""
    return Agent(
        "openai:gpt-4o-mini",
        output_type=Draft,
        system_prompt=(
            "You refine an existing draft based on reviewer feedback. "
            "Keep the same topic and audience. Recompute word_count from body."
        ),
    )

# --- Visibility via iter() --------------------------------------------

def draft_with_visibility(req: DraftRequest) -> Draft:
    """Run the drafter, printing progress as the agent streams its response."""
    print(f"\n[drafter] topic={req.topic!r} audience={req.audience} max_words={req.max_words}")
    with drafter.iter(req.model_dump_json()) as run:
        for node in run:
            if node.is_model_request_node():
                print("  [stream] calling model...")
            elif node.is_call_tools_node():
                print("  [stream] processing tools/output...")
        return run.result.output

def human_review(draft: Draft) -> tuple[Literal["approve", "edit", "reject"], str]:
    """Prompt the human to approve, edit, or reject."""
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print(f"TITLE: {draft.title}")
    print(f"WORDS: {draft.word_count}")
    print("-" * 60)
    print(draft.body)
    print("=" * 60)
    choice = input("Action [approve/edit/reject]: ").strip().lower()
    if choice == "edit":
        feedback = input("What should change? ").strip()
        return "edit", feedback
    return choice, ""  # approve or reject

# --- Main HITL workflow -----------------------------------------------

def workflow(req: DraftRequest, max_revisions: int = 3) -> Draft | None:
    """Run the draft-review loop with up to max_revisions revisions."""
    draft = draft_with_visibility(req)
    for rev in range(max_revisions):
        action, feedback = human_review(draft)
        if action == "approve":
            print(f"\n[workflow] approved after {rev} revision(s).")
            return draft
        if action == "reject":
            print("\n[workflow] rejected by user; aborting.")
            return None
        # edit -> refine
        print(f"\n[workflow] refining (rev {rev + 1}) with feedback: {feedback}")
        refiner = make_refiner()
        result = refiner.run_sync(
            f"Original draft:\n{draft.model_dump_json(indent=2)}\n\n"
            f"Feedback: {feedback}\n\nRefined draft:"
        )
        draft = result.output
    print("\n[workflow] hit max revisions; returning final draft.")
    return draft

if __name__ == "__main__":
    req = DraftRequest(
        topic="Three small habits that improved my focus",
        audience="newsletter readers",
        max_words=180,
    )
    final = workflow(req)
    if final:
        print("\n--- FINAL DRAFT ---")
        print(final.model_dump_json(indent=2))
```

### Walkthrough

**`agent.iter()` for visibility (lines 64-71).** Pydantic AI's `iter()` context manager yields graph nodes as the agent runs. Each node is one of a few types; `is_model_request_node()` and `is_call_tools_node()` are the two you will use most. You can read `node.request` to inspect the actual prompt being sent, or `node.model_response` to see tool calls. The final result lives in `run.result.output`. The reason `iter()` matters for HITL is *trust*: when a human is asked to approve a draft, they want to know the agent actually thought about it and did not just echo the prompt. Streaming progress (even at the granularity of "calling model..." vs "processing tools...") makes the wait feel shorter and the agent feel more deliberate.

**Validator for honesty (lines 21-27).** LLMs routinely miscount words. We add a `field_validator` that recomputes `word_count` from `body` during validation. If the model claims 180 words but wrote 220, the validator fixes it before the draft leaves the agent — guaranteeing downstream code never sees a lying count. This matters in HITL specifically because the human's first instinct on seeing `WORDS: 180` next to a clearly-220-word body is to distrust everything else the agent says. Honest metadata is the foundation of trust.

**Refinement loop (lines 91-104).** The workflow is plain Python. After each draft, we ask the human. On "edit", we build a *fresh* refiner agent (cheap to construct) and pass it the prior draft plus feedback as JSON. Building a new agent per revision keeps the system prompt focused; an alternative is one agent with a `feedback` parameter, but the fresh-agent pattern is easier to reason about because each revision is a clean slate — no risk of prompt-injection-style contamination from prior feedback loops. We also cap revisions at `max_revisions=3` to prevent the human from accidentally creating an infinite loop by always requesting tiny edits.

**No checkpointer needed.** Because the human turn is synchronous Python (`input()`), the agent and the human live in the same process and we never need to persist state across process boundaries. For async or distributed HITL, you would wrap the workflow in a state machine and persist `draft` to a database between turns. The tradeoff: the LangGraph approach (Project 1) gives you persistence for free but adds framework complexity; the Pydantic AI approach (Project 2) is simpler but shifts persistence responsibility to you. Choose based on whether your human reviewer is in the same process (terminal app, Slack bot in same pod) or far away (email-based review, web dashboard with hours-long latency).

### Expected Output

```text
[drafter] topic='Three small habits that improved my focus' audience='newsletter readers' max_words=180
  [stream] calling model...
  [stream] processing tools/output...

============================================================
TITLE: Three Tiny Focus Wins
WORDS: 172
------------------------------------------------------------
For years I struggled with afternoon slumps. Three small changes...
============================================================
Action [approve/edit/reject]: edit
What should change? Add a concrete example for the second habit.

[workflow] refining (rev 1) with feedback: Add a concrete example for the second habit.
  [stream] calling model...
  [stream] processing tools/output...

============================================================
TITLE: Three Tiny Focus Wins
WORDS: 195
------------------------------------------------------------
For years I struggled with afternoon slumps. Three small changes...
============================================================
Action [approve/edit/reject]: approve

[workflow] approved after 1 revision(s).

--- FINAL DRAFT ---
{
  "title": "Three Tiny Focus Wins",
  "body": "For years I struggled with afternoon slumps...",
  "word_count": 195
}
```
